title: 2026-11-07 News
lede: This digest covers about 26 hours, and ICLR 2027 reviews dominated them. ICLR has moved to a new 1–4 scoring scale. A community count of public OpenReview scores finds that 57% of reviews give a 2 and that the median paper averages exactly 2.0. For everything else: Anthropic says AI could take on a median 38% of the researcher time needed to produce a study, and Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, an open model pretrained in under three days.

title: 2026-11-06 News
lede: This digest covers about 28 hours, Thursday to Friday, plus a few older items, and none of it touches peer review or citation analysis. The AI story with the most traction is an Anthropic Claude Code bug report: it says the agent puts the user's email address in the User-Agent header of web-search requests, and it passed a thousand points on Hacker News. Latent Space also revisits its 'Weight-Space Programming' story, the claim that frontier LLMs can write small networks' weights directly; it calls the claim disputed but independently replicated. OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a cybersecurity model.

title: 2026-11-05 News
lede: The weight-space programming story is still the main topic this period, which covers roughly the last 22 hours. The claim is that frontier LLMs can read and write small networks' weights directly, and a highly upvoted rebuttal says the paper overstates it. Separately, TACL will no longer take papers submitted to ARR or other *ACL conferences in the past nine months, including ones that lost the ARR reviewer-capacity lottery.

title: 2026-11-04 News
lede: The day is dominated by "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming," a paper-like blog post by Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab. It claims that frontier LLMs, GPT-6 Astra above all, can read raw neural-network weights to tell what a small network was trained to do, and can edit Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights to improve its math without gradients. A widely shared critique says the post is misleading. Closer to your work: Ehud Reiter sorts LLM-assisted papers into four scenarios, Emily Bender argues against handing peer review's problems to AI, and Ai2's StateBench finds frontier models at 13% or lower on its hardest long-document state-tracking problems.

title: 2026-11-03 News
lede: This covers about a day. The big story is "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming". Its authors claim GPT-6 Astra can read and directly edit the raw weights of a small model. They say it changed only 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and improved its math by up to 6x without any training. The claim comes from a blog post, has not been verified, and reached 2,400+ points on Hacker News. For your citation work, the item to read is a mass replication from the Zou group: it reports that recent LLMs no longer invent citations.

title: 2026-11-02 News
lede: Nothing today touches peer review or citation analysis directly. The most substantial item is a theory preprint arguing that RLVR has no free lunch: when a model specializes in particular strategies, every gain in pass@1 must cost accuracy on some prompt, and the point where pass@k crosses over has a tight bound. The rest is mostly evaluation-methodology posts from the community, an unverified multi-agent coding claim and a few podcasts.

lede: Mistral Large 4 and Gemini 4 Carbon lead today's frontier news, and nothing touches your projects directly. title: 2026-10-29 News
lede: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon leads the day. Google calls it its strongest model, with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities, and Latent Space reports that it tops independent evals while access is limited to trusted cyber defenders at first. Little today touches peer review or citations directly. The closest items are a Reddit thread on whether reviewers should spend compute rerunning paper results, a discussion of whether AI-text detection has a fundamental limit, and Nathan Lambert's look at what benchmarking is missing.

title: 2026-10-28 News
lede: The item closest to your work is AllenAI's blog post on whether LLMs can be trusted to judge if a research idea is novel. Next to it, an r/MachineLearning reviewer for AAAI 2027 and ICLR 2027 estimates that about half of the reviews they can see are AI-generated or AI-edited, though they say they can't prove it. Elsewhere, Anthropic's IPO filing and DeepMind's Genie 4 world model are the big industry stories, and Kevin Buzzard reports that formalising Annals of Mathematics theorems in Lean showed several of them were false as stated.

title: 2026-10-27 News
lede: Three big stories today. OpenAI claims in a preprint that the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false, one of three discoveries it announced in mathematics, computer science and physics, and none of them has been independently verified yet. Anthropic's S-1 filing shows a planned roughly $2T IPO with 85% margins and $1B operating profit in Q2, and OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, a mid-tier model it pitches on writing, visual reasoning and computer use. Nothing in today's batch is directly about peer review or citations; the closest is a paper on stopping agents from dropping correct answers when users push back.
